title: Unraveling Syntax: Language Modeling and the Substructure of Grammars
claim: Total loss decomposes additively into component losses, and components are learned in parallel rather than sequentially.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, left-to-right, curly braces summing component values
description: Two side-by-side line plots of KL divergence against training epochs. Each plot has five colored curves with dots: an orange total-loss curve (L1) that starts highest, and four lower curves for subgrammars L2, L2_2, L2_3 and the constant-string overhead. All curves fall together across training. To the left of each plot, colored curly braces show the initial value of each component (77 against 25, 21, 19 and 12 in panel a; 29.5 against 10, 9.5, 6 and 4 in panel b). The braces visually sum to the total. Panel (a) uses a grammar whose subgrammars each occur 100% of the time. Panel (b) uses a grammar where they occur with probability below 100% (0.3, 0.3, 0.4), and each term is weighted by its probability. Grammar rules are given in italic math in the captions. The eye goes first to the orange curve and the braces.
caption: Experiments visualizing decomposition of KL-divergence (Theorems [ref] and [ref]) over subgrammars, and parallel learning of subgrammars "overhead" refers to constant strings in between subgrammar roots. Full grammars defined in Appendix [ref].
abstract: While language models achieve impressive results, their learning dynamics are far from understood. Many domains of interest -- such as natural language syntax, coding languages, arithmetic -- are captured by context-free grammars (CFGs). In this work, we extend prior work on neural language modeling of CFGs in a novel direction: how language modeling behaves with respect to CFG substructure, namely subgrammars. We define subgrammars, and prove a set of fundamental theorems connecting language modeling and subgrammars. We show that language modeling loss recurses linearly over its top-level subgrammars; applied recursively, the loss decomposes into losses for "irreducible" subgrammars. Under additional assumptions, and empirically, parametrized models learn subgrammars in parallel, unlike children who first master simple substructures. We find that subgrammar pretraining can improve final performance, but only for tiny models relative to the grammar, while alignment analyses show that pretraining consistently leads to internal representations that better reflect the grammar's substructure.
